extracted.intended_audience: educated subscribers/readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or assessing short, moral-philosophical essays for a periodical (Spectator-style) that mix anecdote, moral reflection, and social commentary. Emphasizes clarity, persuasive moral argument, examples, and gentle satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Tom Dread-Nought (ambition/spleen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tom Dread-Nought's heart: active, shoots up and down in its phial; the fomes (spot) is small, red and fiery, causing violent agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as a man who behaved well in war but for ten years has been consumed by ambition for posts of honour, retired to the country and become choked with spleen and choler — jealous, railing at better men and perpetually uneasy because he thinks his merit unrewarded. Use as a character-indicator: restless agitation + small fiery blemish = thwarted ambition and sourness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Dick Gloomy (avarice → melancholy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dick Gloomy's heart: remarkably small, lies still at the bottom of the phial, beating scarcely at all; the fomes is quite black and spreads over the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents a man who thirsts only for money but remains poor; avarice has thrown him into melancholy and despair. Use as a cautionary exemplar: excessive love of money produces listlessness, envy, idleness, and hatred of mankind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Will Worthy (noble soul with vanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large fair heart that beats strongly; the fomes/spot is exceedingly small and always appears in the strongest point of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents a noble-souled person possessing many good qualities, with only a tiny speck of vanity. Use as an evaluative criterion: dominant good qualities with only minor vanities denote an admirable character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Freelove (passion mistaken for rancour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freelove's heart initially appears overcast with rancour to the observer, but closer inspection shows the small swelling spot to be only Passion, which disappears on nearer view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lesson: superficial impressions of others' hearts can be mistaken; apparent ill-will may be passion or misread feeling. Moral: inspect carefully before judging a friend's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Coquetilla (coquetry signified by many-coloured fomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A female heart with the fomes of the largest size and of a hundred different colours, varying every moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as the heart of a coquette; large, multicoloured, changeable blemish = flirtatious, capricious behaviour. Use as a typology for female coquetry in character sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Melissa (prude whose blemish grows on inspection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A heart whose fomes appears very small at first but, on steady looking, grows larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents Melissa, a noted prude; the growing spot suggests hypocrisy or repressed passion revealed under scrutiny. Use as an example of hidden faults becoming evident under closer examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: Seraphina (spotless innocence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A crystal-clear heart with no perceivable blemish; if any blemish exists it is too small for human eyes to discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents exceptional innocence and purity; contrasted with other female acquaintances who have large 'blue' spots. Use as the idealized exemplar of moral innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart-vision: female hearts with twisted veins = deceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Many examined female hearts show the fomes running in several veins twisted together into a perplexed figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interpreter explains this figure as representing deceit. Use as an allegorical symbol — convoluted veining/patching in the heart indicates duplicity and guile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of disinterested benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Benevolence is shown by spontaneous pity (even in children and thoughtless people) and by the immediate delight of giving or relieving distress, not by calculated self-interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments advanced: (1) pity arises without reflection and in those incapable of self-interested calculation; (2) the pleasure from doing good is distinct from selfish reward and is evidence of genuine benevolence; (3) benevolence and self-love are compatible, but benevolence is nevertheless unselfish. Use these tests when judging whether an action or disposition is truly altruistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical 'articles' on Eternity and God's existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Four declarative articles: (1) No being could have made itself; (2) therefore some being must have existed from all eternity; (3) created beings, as we conceive existence, could not have existed from eternity; (4) that eternal being must be the great Author of Nature — the Ancient of Days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a reasoned 'creed of a philosopher' about Eternity: these premises are used to argue for a necessary, eternal Creator distinct in mode of existence from created things. Use as a structure for metaphysical argument: start from conceivability/contradiction, infer necessity, distinguish modes of existence, and conclude transcendence of the divine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic modesty in divine speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejects attempts to explain God's manner of existence (e.g., 'eternity is a punctum stans' or 'infinite instance') as words without ideas; recommends owning ignorance rather than advancing self-contradictory doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for writers/philosophers: when discussing the divine or truly incomprehensible subjects, prefer modest acknowledgement of limits of human conceptions; avoid asserting metaphysical formulations that have no intelligible content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden/landscape principle: preserve venerable trees and wood
rubrics_metrics.description: Author prefers leaving the space between walks as much a wood as found it; values oaks of four hundred years and elms that might shelter a troop of horse over tulips or carnations; criticises prodigal heirs who fell ancient trees and ruin the product of ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical aesthetic guidance for country-seat landscaping: prioritize existing ancient trees and woodland character over ornamental bedding; preserve ancestral trees as monuments of industry and history; view felling as wasteful and injurious to landscape continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for sacred/protected trees (Hamadryad tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients regarded certain trees as protected by deities (e.g., Dodona, Delphi groves) and considered it sacrilege to injure them; the Hamadryad myth ties a nymph's life to a tree and praises those who preserve trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/moral argument for tree preservation: appeals to tradition and myth to legitimise respect for venerable trees and to encourage protective behaviour. Use anecdote (Rhoecus and the Hamadryad) to illustrate gratitude and reciprocal obligations with nature; warns against abusing such spirits or their symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love-casuist maxims (rules for judging amorous behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of aphoristic maxims about love and lovers: e.g., 'There are more Calamities in the World arising from Love than from Hatred'; 'Love is the Daughter of Idleness, but the Mother of Disquietude'; distinctions about constancy across temperaments and ages; remarks on coquetry, prudery, and the effects of reviving passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as practical, humorous guidelines a 'love casuist' might use to adjudicate amorous questions (what counts as a squeeze of the fingers, a denial, permitted advances, meaning of smiles/frowns). Use these maxims and situational rules for social commentary, satire, or as a resource for composing comic/observational passages about courtship.
